messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 70
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Witnessed other trauma
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Temperature): A specific temperature on the skin, Media / News: Related news, Loss of Control: Lack of control
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me, Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: No Accountability: The people responsible have faced no consequences, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Lucía Herrera is a 70-year-old Mexican American fashion designer who has been married for more than four decades and still spends most weekdays in the garment studio she founded in Los Angeles. She came to treatment after months of telling herself she should be able to carry on, only to find that ordinary moments in the studio, at home, and even in conversations with her husband could suddenly collapse into the same scene she has been trying not to revisit. The event she returns to is the violent death of someone she loved, a loss she witnessed at close range and has never been able to place safely in the past.

She describes that day in fragments that arrive with disturbing completeness. She and this person had been together when an assault unfolded quickly, with shouting, confusion, and the sickening realization that events were moving faster than she could influence them. What remains most unbearable to Lucía is not only that she saw the injury and the aftermath, but that she remembers the bodily shock of it: the feel of air on her skin, a sudden, unmistakable temperature that now seems burned into the memory. She remembers trying to do something, trying to get control of what was happening and failing. In the middle of the chaos she had the conviction that if she moved differently, spoke faster, insisted harder, or somehow placed herself between danger and the other person, the outcome might have changed. The people she believes were responsible were never meaningfully held to account. That fact has remained fixed in her mind with a hard, unresolved bitterness.

In the weeks afterward, Lucía found that the memory did not behave like a recollection. It forced itself into her mind without invitation. She could be pinning fabric on a dress form, warming her hands around a cup, or stepping from one room to another when something in the temperature against her skin would bring everything back at once. In those moments it did not feel like thinking about the event; it felt as though she was there again, with the same sensory immediacy, the same bodily certainty that something terrible was happening. She would freeze in place in her workroom, fingers still holding a measuring tape, while the studio around her disappeared behind the full reality of that scene. She has learned to dread the speed of it. What frightens her most is that there is no warning: a shift in heat or coolness, a news report playing from a television in the reception area, any situation in which she feels she is not in control, and suddenly the whole memory is present across all her senses.

Over time, her life narrowed around efforts not to brush against anything that might bring on that return. She stopped watching the news entirely after realizing that reports of violence and loss could ruin the rest of her day. In her studio, where assistants often stream morning coverage while they work, she began asking for televisions to be turned off and would leave the room if she overheard certain headlines. She also started refusing memorial gatherings, family conversations about the person who died, and even small domestic acts that felt like grief reminders. If her husband took out old photographs or mentioned an anniversary, she would redirect him or leave the room, telling herself she could not afford to fall apart. She has also become wary of feeling too happy. A successful show, a warm dinner with family, even a rare lighthearted afternoon can make her pull back abruptly. Positive emotion feels unsafe to her, as though letting herself feel good would leave her exposed, careless, or somehow disloyal.

Lucía speaks about the event with a steady stream of blame turned inward. She has come to believe that she failed in the most important duty she had in that moment: to protect someone vulnerable. She says she should have known more, acted faster, controlled the situation better. When she says this, she does not present it as a passing doubt but as a settled verdict. Alongside that is a cold fury that those responsible have faced no consequences. The world, as she experiences it now, feels capable of allowing terrible things to happen without answer, and that recognition sits beside her conviction that she herself acted wrongly.

These patterns have had visible costs. In the business she once ran with elegance and spontaneity, she is now rigid about the studio environment and reluctant to attend industry events where screens, crowds, and unpredictability are unavoidable. At home, her husband has felt the distance created by her refusal to speak about the loss and by the way she shuts down moments of pleasure just when the two of them seem most connected. She finally sought help after being overtaken by the memory at work when a sudden change in temperature on her skin left her gripping a cutting table, unable to orient for several minutes while younger staff looked on in alarm. She says she is tired of living at the mercy of moments she cannot predict. What she fears most is that the memory will keep arriving with the same force forever, and that she will die still believing she failed the person she could not save. What she hopes for, more quietly, is to be able to remember without being thrown back into the event and to sit with her husband in peace without bracing for the next intrusion.
